content:
Quick answer: Strength training is beneficial for arthritis, reducing pain and improving function. A beginner programme could include wall push-ups, seated leg extensions, and resistance band rows for weeks 1–2. Progress to chair squats and step-ups in weeks 3–4. Always warm up, avoid training through sharp pain, and allow 48 hours rest between sessions for the same muscle group.

Why Strength Matters

Strong muscles absorb shock and stabilise joints, reducing the load on damaged cartilage. Systematic reviews in The Lancet Rheumatology and elsewhere consistently show that regular resistance training meaningfully reduces knee OA pain over time, which is why it is a core recommendation in NICE guidance for managing osteoarthritis.

The 4-Week Starter Programme

Week 1–2: Foundation

  • Wall push-ups: 2 sets × 8 reps
  • Seated leg extensions: 2 sets × 10 reps
  • Standing calf raises: 2 sets × 12 reps
  • Resistance band rows: 2 sets × 8 reps

Week 3–4: Progression

  • Chair squats: 2 sets × 10 reps
  • Resistance band chest press: 2 sets × 10 reps
  • Step-ups (low step): 2 sets × 8 per leg
  • Plank hold: 2 × 15 seconds

Golden Rules

  1. Never train through sharp pain — dull ache during exercise is acceptable
  2. Apply the 24-hour rule: if a joint is more swollen or painful 24 hours after exercise, you did too much
  3. Warm up first: 5 minutes of gentle movement
  4. Rest days matter: allow 48 hours between sessions for the same muscle group

Programme by Sarah Mitchell, MCSP, HCPC Registered Physiotherapist

What the Evidence Says

Extensive high-quality research shows that regular strength training is incredibly beneficial for people living with various forms of arthritis. Systematic reviews, which combine results from many different studies, consistently find that strengthening exercises lead to significant reductions in pain, improved physical function, and a better quality of life. These benefits are seen across different joints and types of arthritis.

Clinical guidelines from leading rheumatology organisations universally recommend incorporating strength training into arthritis management plans. These recommendations are based on strong evidence from randomised controlled trials, which are considered the gold standard in medical research. They show that supervised, progressive resistance exercise is not only effective but also safe when performed correctly.

The improvements aren't just about feeling better; studies also indicate that strengthening muscles around arthritic joints can slow down disease progression in some cases, by stabilising the joint and helping to protect the cartilage from further wear and tear.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting too heavy too soon: Begin with easily manageable weights or bodyweight to establish good form.
  • Holding your breath: Breathe out during the effort part of the exercise and in during the recovery.
  • Skipping warm-ups or cool-downs: Always prepare your body and gently wind down to prevent stiffness.
  • Only focusing on one muscle group: Aim for a balanced programme that works all major muscle groups.
  • Not listening to your body: Differentiate between muscle fatigue and joint pain. If a joint hurts, stop.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While strength training is generally very safe and beneficial, there are times when it's really important to get advice from a healthcare professional. If you experience new or worsening symptoms that are beyond what you'd expect from typical muscle soreness, or if you're uncertain about how to exercise safely with your particular type of arthritis, please reach out to your doctor, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist.

You should seek advice if you experience:

  • Sudden, severe joint pain that doesn't settle.
  • Increased joint swelling, redness, or warmth that lasts more than 24 hours.
  • New numbness, tingling, or weakness in a limb.
  • Pain that wakes you up at night or is present at rest.
  • Difficulty performing daily tasks due to exercise-related joint issues.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should I lift weights if I have arthritis?

For most people, two to three sessions per week targeting the major muscle groups is ideal. This allows sufficient time for muscle recovery and adaptation, which is crucial for building strength and preventing overuse.

Can strength training make my arthritis worse?

When done correctly and progressively, strength training is highly unlikely to make your arthritis worse. In fact, it typically improves symptoms. The key is to start gently, listen to your body, and never push through sharp pain, always respecting the 24-hour rule.

Do I need to buy special equipment for strength training?

Not at all! Many effective strength exercises can be done using just your body weight, such as squats, lunges, and push-ups against a wall. Resistance bands are also an excellent, affordable way to add challenge, and household items like full water bottles can serve as light weights.

Practical next steps for Strength Training with Arthritis: A Beginner's Safe Start Guide

If you came here about Strength Training with Arthritis: A Beginner's Safe Start Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Quick questions about Strength Training with Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
